_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 5 Inside Your Body. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (organs; the brain and the lungs; the heart; the stomach and the intestine; models of the body, here as the diagram and then the lung model), in the lesson's own words, drawn with the lesson's own picture of the organs (ART.figure 'organs', the figure the child taps in the Organ finder and labels in the Body diagram) and with the bottle-and-balloon model the child builds two steps later.
title: Inside Your Body
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Identify some of the important organs in humans (limited to brain, heart, stomach, intestine and lungs) and describe their functions.
Know that there are different types of models in science, including diagrams and physical models that we can touch.

beats.say: Inside you, right now, five organs are hard at work.
Each one has a job. Your body needs every one of them.
An organ is a part inside your body with a job to do.
You cannot see them with your eyes. Here is where they sit.
Today you will meet five. The brain, in your head. The lungs, in your chest.
The heart between the lungs, the stomach, and the intestine below.
The brain sits in your head, inside your skull.
It thinks. It remembers. It feels.
And it tells every other part of you what to do.
The lungs are in your chest. They take air in when you breathe in.
They push it out again when you breathe out, all day long.
The heart sits between your two lungs, in the middle of your chest.
Many children put it on the far left. It is really in the middle.
The heart is a pump. About once a second, it squeezes.
Each squeeze pushes blood round your whole body.
Blood carries food, and the goodness from the air, to every part of you.
Put a hand on your chest and feel it beating.
When you swallow, food goes down to your stomach.
The stomach is a stretchy bag. It churns the food into mush.
The stomach is not your whole tummy. It is one bag, up under your ribs.
Then the mush moves into the intestine, a long coiled tube.
The goodness passes through its walls and into your blood.
We cannot look inside ourselves, so scientists use models.
A diagram is one kind of model. It is a drawing with labels.
Today you will put five labels on a picture of the body.
Brain, lungs, heart, stomach, intestine. That is a diagram.
Another kind of model is one you can make and touch.
A grown-up cuts the bottom off a bottle. The bottle is your chest.
A balloon hangs inside it, from the neck. That balloon is a lung.
A second balloon stretches across the bottom. That is the breathing muscle.
Pull the bottom balloon down, and the lung fills with air. Breathing in.
Let go, and the lung empties. Breathing out. Your model breathes.
Brain thinks. Lungs breathe. Heart pumps blood.
The stomach breaks food down. The intestine takes the goodness.
A diagram and a bottle of balloons are both models of your body.
Five organs, five jobs, all working inside you right now.
